2024 · EMNLP 2024 · Agents

DA-Code: Agent Data Science Code Generation Benchmark for Large Language Models

A 500-task benchmark that drops LLM agents into a real Docker sandbox with messy, multi-file data — Bash, Python, and SQL, no scaffolding shortcuts — and grades them by executing the code they write. The best pairing tested, GPT-4 driving the paper's own DA-Agent scaffold, clears only 30.5%.

// the gap

What problem is this solving?

Prior data-science code-generation benchmarks frame the task as instruction-to-code translation: DS-1000 is a 1,000-example code-completion benchmark over a single file, graded with Pass@K; Arcade is a 1,078-example notebook-completion benchmark, graded by output match. Neither runs the model in a controllable, executable environment, and neither requires planning — Table 1's own comparison marks both "✗" on "Control. Exec. Env?" and "Need Planning?". MLAgentBench moves to an interactive, plannable setting but stays narrow: 13 instances, framed as whole "ML Project" runs. DA-Bench (InfiAgent-DABench) puts the model in a controllable environment for CSV analysis, but with a single file per task, 257 instances, and — like DS-1000 and Arcade — no planning requirement and an output-match grader.

DA-Code's authors argue that none of these look like how a data analyst actually works: exploring an unfamiliar, noisy set of resources (databases, spreadsheets, documents, code — "beyond just a notebook environment"), deciding what to use, writing and debugging code iteratively, and only then producing an answer. DA-Code operationalizes that as 500 tasks averaging 5.7 files per task and 85 lines of reference solution code, run inside an executable sandbox, requiring planning, and graded by execution rather than string match — one of only two benchmarks in Table 1 with "✓" on both "Control. Exec. Env?" and "Need Planning?" (the other being MLAgentBench, at 13 instances).

// how it works

The method

Ten annotators "highly proficient in data analysis, SQL, and Python" build DA-Code through a five-stage pipeline (Figure 2): (1) manually select data sources from Kaggle, GitHub, and other web sources against four principles — real-world relevance, complexity, timeliness, and coding intensity; (2) either rewrite an existing task's explicit code instructions into an abstract natural-language agent instruction, or manually annotate a new task over those same discovered resources (the paper notes most tasks come from the rewrite route); (3) implement the task inside a Docker sandbox, deliberately keeping the initial resources noisy — the running example turns a handful of databases into a multi-file workspace by adding supporting docs like data_standard.md and schema.yml the agent has to read to figure out what it needs; (4) write a per-task evaluation configuration (table-, chart-, or text-based); and (5) cross-validate the task design and run red-team tests "to determine if there are any false positives or false negatives."

Tasks split into three categories in roughly a 1:1:3 ratio: Data Wrangling (cleaning, loading, transforming raw files/databases), Machine Learning (classification, regression, clustering — restricted to "traditional machine learning algorithms... no deep learning methods allowed"), and Exploratory Data Analysis (data manipulation, data insights, visualization, statistical analysis, using SQL and Python together).

The paper's own agent baseline, DA-Agent, runs inside a Docker-based Linux sandbox pre-loaded with Python, SQL, Conda, and database engines. Rather than the usual edit-then-execute two-step loop, its action space fuses editing and execution into single actions — Bash(command), Python(save_path, code), SQL(file_path, command, output), and Terminate(output) — to cut down on interaction steps. Episodes run greedy decoding for up to 20 steps, a memory window that by default keeps the last 15 steps of history (ablated at 10 and 5), and a 300-second execution timeout per action.

Grading is per-output-type rather than a single blanket metric. Table outputs get a binary table match score: the predicted CSV/database/JSON is compared column-by-column against the reference on exactly the columns the instruction specifies, and any discrepancy scores 0 — an unqualified exact match. Chart outputs get a binary chart match score: rather than judging the rendered image, the evaluation embeds an extraction script into the model's own plotting code to pull out both the numerical data and the plot configuration (title, axis labels, legend), and requires both to match the reference exactly (with sorting/scaling tolerance on the data when the instruction doesn't pin down order or scale). Machine-learning outputs get an ML normalized score that maps whatever raw metric applies (F1, MAE, Silhouette Score, etc.) onto a common 0–1 scale:

Score = min(1, max(0, ŝ − SbaselineSbest − Sbaseline)) // ŝ = the model's raw metric value; S_best / S_baseline bound the 0–1 range per task
// what they found

The results

Seven models were run through DA-Agent on the full 500-task benchmark (Table 3, below). The headline number — "the current best LLMs achieves only 30.5% accuracy," per the abstract — is GPT-4 + DA-Agent's Total score of 30.5. GPT-4 posts the best Total, ML (48.4), EDA (24.6), Medium-difficulty (27.8), Hard-difficulty (23.4), and Completion Rate (99.4%) among all seven; on the scored and rate columns, GPT-4o edges ahead only on Data-Wrangling score (33.3 vs. 30.4), Easy-difficulty score (46.2 vs. 45.4), and Executable-Code rate (77.7% vs. 76.8%) — despite that, GPT-4o's own Total (29.1) trails GPT-4's, a reminder that a newer, more code-fluent model isn't automatically the stronger agent on this benchmark. Closed-source models (GPT-4 30.5, GPT-4o 29.1, Claude-3-Opus 27.6) clear a substantially wider margin over open-source ones (Qwen2.5-72B 22.6, Deepseek-Coder-V2.5 20.7, Mixtral-8x22B 15.4, Deepseek-Coder-33B 10.8) than their Executable Code rates alone would suggest — Qwen2.5-72B's code runs about as reliably as Claude-3-Opus's (72.2% vs. 75.7%) but its Total score is 5 points lower, meaning the gap is more about whether the actions solve the task than whether the code executes. Performance falls from Easy to Medium to Hard for six of the seven models; the exception is Qwen2.5-72B, whose Hard-difficulty score (22.3) is actually higher than its own Medium-difficulty score (19.4).

A second experiment (Table 4, included above) isolates the scaffold rather than the model: on a random 100-task subset (DA-Code-100), GPT-4 is paired with four different agent frameworks. DA-Agent scores 31.5 with a 99.5% completion rate, ahead of OpenDevin (26.2 / 96.0%), AutoGen (18.6 / 78.8%), and X-Agent (6.7 / 38.7%) — all under the identical model and task set. OpenDevin's completion rate (96.0%) is close to DA-Agent's, but its score is 5.3 points lower, so finishing a task and scoring on it are not the same thing. Giving DA-Agent a human-annotated reference plan lifts GPT-4's score further to 39.7 (completion rate actually dips slightly to 97.7%); the paper reads this as evidence that "planning ability [is] a key performance factor" — the sharper "not raw code execution" contrast is our own reading of the gap, not a claim the paper makes. By contrast, shrinking DA-Agent's memory window from the default 15 steps to 10 (32.3) or 5 (30.8) barely moves the score.

Across trajectories (Figure 5, not shown), success rates climb quickly over the first 5–10 steps and then plateau, while incompletion rates keep declining more slowly through step 20 — the paper's own reading is that "additional steps do not necessarily lead to successful outcomes." A step-by-step action-type breakdown (their "EEEA" — Exploration, Execution, Evaluation, Adjustment — pattern) shows stronger models like GPT-4 and GPT-4o shifting from file-viewing actions toward debugging actions as an episode progresses, while Deepseek-Coder keeps re-exploring files later into its trajectories. The paper's qualitative error analysis names four recurring failure modes: incorrect assumptions about the environment such as presuming file names, non-standard or malformed action syntax, getting stuck in debugging loops on persistent code errors, and premature termination from misreading the task.

// does it hold up?

The eval read

DA-Code is a genuine step up in rigor from single-shot code-completion benchmarks — Table 1's own side-by-side against DS-1000, Arcade, MLAgentBench, and DA-Bench is a fair comparison, and grading by execution rather than string match is the right instinct for agentic tasks. Two things still deserve scrutiny before taking the 30.5% headline at face value.

The framework comparison in Table 4 (DA-Agent vs. OpenDevin, AutoGen, X-Agent) is run on only the 100-task DA-Code-100 subset and only with GPT-4 as the base model; the paper doesn't say whether the competing frameworks' prompts were tuned to the same degree DA-Agent's own was, and there's no check of whether DA-Agent's edge over OpenDevin (31.5 vs. 26.2) survives with a weaker open-source model or on the full 500 tasks. Separately, nowhere does the paper mention contamination, decontamination, or a training-cutoff cross-check, despite mining Kaggle and GitHub for "timely" data late in 2024 — and its own Appendix A.2 worked example is a "Bank customer data for churn prediction" task built on files named Churn_Modelling.csv — to our own knowledge (not a claim the paper makes) a widely reproduced, multi-year-old public Kaggle dataset, the kind of thing plausibly present in the pretraining data of every model under test. The paper's four source-selection principles (real-world relevance, complexity, timeliness, coding intensity) address freshness of the source but never address whether "timely" collection actually keeps a task's reference solution out of a frontier model's training corpus.

The grading itself is strict binary exact-match for table and chart outputs (table score = 1 only if the predicted table equals the reference on the specified columns; chart score = 1 only if both the data and the plot configuration match). That's a defensible design for well-specified tasks, but the paper's own "Data Insights" category is explicitly described as tasks that "do not provide clear solutions, necessitating thoughtful consideration and autonomous decision-making" — for exactly that open-ended slice, a differently-formatted but reasonable answer scores identically to a wrong one, and the red-team process that's supposed to catch grader false positives/negatives is described only qualitatively ("cross validation... to determine if there are any false positives or false negatives"), with no rate reported. Worth flagging too: the paper's "Machine Learning" category explicitly forbids deep-learning solutions ("only traditional machine learning algorithms... no deep learning methods allowed"), which is reasonable for keeping the normalized-score formula well-defined but means the reported ML column — the single highest-scoring category for every model in Table 3 — says nothing about deep-learning pipeline agency, despite the category's broad name.

baselines

DA-Agent beats OpenDevin/AutoGen/X-Agent under GPT-4 on a 100-task subset only; no cross-check with a second base model or the full 500-task set, and prompt-tuning parity across frameworks isn't documented.

contamination

Not discussed. Sourced from Kaggle/GitHub with a "timeliness" principle but no decontamination check; the paper's own worked ML example uses a well-known public Kaggle churn dataset (Churn_Modelling.csv).

what's missed

Binary exact-match table/chart grading gives no partial credit on the benchmark's own "open-ended" Data Insights tasks; red-teamed false-positive/negative rate is described but never quantified; the "Machine Learning" category explicitly excludes deep learning.

would raise confidence

A quantified grader false-positive/negative rate; an explicit contamination or leakage analysis; named model snapshots/dates and decoding settings beyond "greedy sampling"; the Table 4 framework comparison repeated on more than one base model and the full task set; and a fix to the Table 2 vs. Figure 7 mismatch on the Visualization/Statistical-Analysis split.

// bottom line

A believable, humbling 30.5% ceiling from a benchmark that is measurably more agentic than its predecessors — but the paper is silent on contamination for a late-2024 benchmark built from public Kaggle/GitHub data, and on how strict its own strict-match graders actually are in practice, which is exactly the kind of gap that should make a reader treat the headline number as an upper rather than a precise bound.

// takeaways

What to remember

  1. DA-Code turns data-science code generation into a 500-task agent benchmark — a Docker sandbox, Bash/Python/SQL actions, and execution-based grading — rather than single-file code completion. Table 1's own comparison makes the jump from DS-1000/Arcade concrete: 5.7 files per task on average (vs. 1), 85 average lines of reference solution, and required planning.
  2. Even the strongest pairing tested — GPT-4 driving the paper's own DA-Agent scaffold — clears only 30.5% overall. DA-Agent's scaffold itself beats OpenDevin (26.2), AutoGen (18.6), and X-Agent (6.7) under the same GPT-4 model on a 100-task subset, and handing it a human-written reference plan pushes GPT-4 to 39.7 — evidence the paper reads as planning ability being a key performance factor.
  3. Watch the eval-rigor gaps before quoting the headline number: no contamination analysis for a benchmark mined from public Kaggle/GitHub data in late 2024 (including a recognizable Kaggle churn dataset in the paper's own worked example), no quantified rate for the red-teamed grader false positives/negatives behind a strict binary exact-match scorer, and a Table 2/Figure 7 internal inconsistency in the reported EDA task-type split.
